Following the Royal Assent of Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1, S.C. 2026, c. 3) on March 26, 2026, Canada's federal SR&ED regime has undergone its most substantial legislative expansion in over a decade. Effective for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% refundable Investment Tax Credit (ITC) has doubled from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000 (surpassing the $4,500,000 interim proposal from the December 16, 2024 Fall Economic Statement), allowing qualifying corporations to claim up to $2,100,000 annually in fully refundable federal credits on current expenditures. Concurrently, Bill C-15 expanded the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds from $10,000,000– $50,000,000 to $15,000,000– $75,000,000, extended access to the 35% enhanced refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) using a three-year average gross revenue phase-out test (which Canadian-controlled private corporations [CCPCs] may also elect to use), and restored the SR&ED eligibility of capital expenditures, shared-use equipment (SUE), and equipment lease costs for property acquired or lease obligations incurred after December 15, 2024.

At the provincial level, significant legislative divergences require rigorous multi-jurisdictional modelling. Quebec abolished eight legacy R&D tax measures—including its former R&D salary tax credit—for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, replacing them with the unified Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC), which provides a 30% refundable credit on the first $1,000,000 of eligible R&D, pre-commercialization, and capital equipment expenditures above an exclusion threshold, and 20% on the excess. British Columbia expressly aligned with the federal Bill C-15 reforms (adopting the $6,000,000 expenditure limit, ECPC eligibility, and capital expenditure restoration while making its 10% credit permanent), Ontario restored 100% of qualified capital expenditures to its Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC, 8%) and Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC, 3.5%) bases effective December 16, 2024 while retaining its $3,000,000 OITC expenditure cap, and Saskatchewan doubled its 10% refundable CCPC expenditure threshold from $1,000,000 to $2,000,000. Furthermore, effective April 1, 2026, the CRA launched a formal, optional Pre-Claim Approval Process offering upfront technical eligibility determinations within eight weeks and cutting post-filing expenditure review processing times in half from 180 days to 90 calendar days.
1. Statutory and Legislative Architecture of the Canadian SR&ED Program
1.1 Dual-Incentive Statutory Structure under the Income Tax Act

Canada's federal Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax incentive program is codified in the federal Income Tax Act (ITA), R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), and Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations (C.R.C., c. 945). Administered jointly by the Department of Finance Canada (which formulates tax policy and legislative amendments) and the Canada Revenue Agency (which executes technical, scientific, and financial compliance reviews), the SR&ED program is the largest single source of federal support for industrial R&D in Canada, disbursing $4.6 billion in allowed Investment Tax Credits across 23,677 processed claims in the 2025–2026 fiscal year (and $4.5 billion across 22,738 processed claims in 2024–2025).

Unlike discretionary government grants that are constrained by fixed parliamentary appropriations and competitive application windows, the SR&ED program is a statutory entitlement embedded within Canada's self-assessment income tax system. Any taxpayer carrying on a business in Canada that performs qualifying SR&ED work in Canada—and satisfies the mandatory statutory reporting deadlines—is legally entitled to two distinct, interlocking tax incentives.

First, Section 37 of the Income Tax Act establishes the SR&ED Expenditure Deduction Pool. Under subsection 37(1), a taxpayer carrying on business in Canada may deduct current SR&ED expenditures—and, for property acquired after December 15, 2024, qualifying SR&ED capital expenditures—in computing net income from the business for the taxation year. Rather than expiring at year-end or converting immediately into ordinary non-capital losses, undeducted SR&ED expenditures accumulate in an indefinite-life pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures that may be carried forward indefinitely to reduce taxable income in any future taxation year. This indefinite carryforward is subject to two primary statutory exceptions: (a) if a corporation or trust undergoes a loss restriction event (an acquisition of control), subsection 37(6.1) restricts future deductions of pre-acquisition pool balances to income from that same or a similar business; and (b) under paragraph 96(1)(e.1), a partnership cannot carry forward an unused SR&ED expenditure pool to a subsequent fiscal period, but must deduct 100% of its available pool in computing partnership net income or loss in the year incurred.

Second, Sections 127 and 127.1 of the Income Tax Act establish the SR&ED Investment Tax Credit (ITC) regime. Under subsections 127(5), 127(9), and 127(10.1), a taxpayer earns an ITC calculated as a percentage (15% basic rate or 35% enhanced rate) of its SR&ED qualified expenditure pool at the end of the taxation year. Earned ITCs are first applied to reduce federal Part I income tax otherwise payable in the current taxation year. Depending on the legal classification of the claimant and whether the underlying expenditure is current or capital in nature, remaining unused ITCs may either be refunded in cash under section 127.1 or carried back 3 taxation years and carried forward 20 taxation years to offset federal Part I tax payable.

To prevent double-dipping between the subsection 37(1) income deduction and the section 127 tax credit, paragraph 37(1)(e) of the Income Tax Act mandates that any SR&ED ITC deducted against Part I tax payable or refunded in cash in a taxation year (including ITCs earned on the notional Prescribed Proxy Amount) must be subtracted from the taxpayer's subsection 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures in the immediately following taxation year (reported on Line 435 of Form T661). Because this pool reduction occurs in the subsequent taxation year rather than the year the credit is earned, the taxpayer only pays corporate income tax on the credit amount in the following year. If the subtraction of prior-year ITCs under paragraph 37(1)(e) and current-year government or non-government assistance under paragraph 37(1)(d) causes the subsection 37(1) pool balance to become negative at year-end, paragraph 12(1)(v) requires the negative balance to be included directly in the taxpayer's business income for that year, while paragraph 37(1)(c.1) restores the pool balance to nil in the following taxation year.

body.text: 2. Scientific and Technological Eligibility Framework
2.1 The Core Statutory Definition (Subsection 248(1) ITA)

The foundational gateway to every federal and provincial R&D tax claim in Canada is the definition of "scientific research and experimental development" in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act (which remained unchanged by Bill C-15). The opening preamble and paragraphs (a) through (c) establish the core eligible work categories:

"scientific research and experimental development" means systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis and that is (a) basic research, namely, work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view, (b) applied research, namely, work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view, or (c) experimental development, namely, work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products or processes, including incremental improvements thereto...

Across Canadian industrial claimants—where software development alone accounts for 40.8% of allowed SR&ED tax credits according to practitioner analysis of CRA statistics, alongside major concentrations in manufacturing, biotechnology, clean technology, and materials engineering—the vast majority of corporate SR&ED projects fall under paragraph (c) experimental development, with the remainder falling under paragraph (b) applied research (such as pre-clinical biotechnology investigations or novel vaccine development with a targeted practical application) or paragraph (a) basic research (pure theoretical or laboratory inquiry without a specific practical application in view). Crucially, the statutory phrase "including incremental improvements thereto" in paragraph (c) confirms that an experimental development project does not need to create a revolutionary, industry-first invention; evolutionary and incremental improvements to existing products, manufacturing lines, or software architectures qualify provided they seek a genuine technological advancement through systematic experimentation or analysis.
2.2 Eligible Support Work (Paragraph 248(1)(d)) vs. Statutory Exclusions (Paragraphs 248(1)(e)–(k))
Once a core project is established under paragraph (a), (b), or (c), paragraph 248(1)(d) expands the scope of eligible SR&ED to include specific supporting activities:

...and, in applying this definition in respect of a taxpayer, includes (d) work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing or psychological research, where the work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of work described in paragraph (a), (b), or (c) that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer...

For support work to qualify under paragraph 248(1)(d), three strict statutory conditions must be satisfied simultaneously. First, the activity must fall within one of the eight closed statutory categories: engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research. Second, the work must be directly in support of resolving the scientific or technological uncertainty of the core basic research, applied research, or experimental development project carried on in Canada. Third, the scale, duration, and quantity of the support work must be commensurate with the needs of the core research or experimental development. Any design, coding, fabrication, or production beyond what is necessary to execute the experiment or analysis constitutes commercial development or excess production and must be carved out from the claim.

Conversely, paragraphs 248(1)(e) through (k) establish seven absolute statutory exclusions. Even if performed within the broader timeline of an otherwise eligible R&D project, work with respect to any of these seven categories is excluded work and never qualifies as SR&ED. body.text: 2.3 The Five Jurisprudence Criteria (Northwest Hydraulic) and the CRA's Two-Step "Why and How" Methodology

For over two decades, Canadian courts and the CRA have evaluated SR&ED eligibility using the five-question common law test formulated by Judge Bowman (later Chief Justice of the Tax Court of Canada) in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1839, [1998] 3 CTC 2520 (TCC), and affirmed by the Federal Court of Appeal in RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen, 99 DTC 5087 (FCA), C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393, and Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. The Queen, 2021 FCA 88:

items: Technological Risk or Uncertainty: Was there a technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures? If the resolution of the problem is reasonably predictable using techniques, procedures, and data generally accessible to competent professionals in the field, there is no technological uncertainty.

Formulation of Hypotheses: Did the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty? Judge Bowman defined this as a five-stage process: (a) observation of the subject matter of the problem; (b) formulation of a clear objective; (c) identification and articulation of the technological uncertainty; (d) formulation of a hypothesis or hypotheses designed to reduce or eliminate the uncertainty; and (e) methodical and systematic testing of the hypotheses.

Accordance with the Scientific Method: Did the procedures adopted accord with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses? The approach must be characterized by trained and systematic observation, measurement, and experiment, rather than intuitive trial-and-error or haphazard tinkering.

Technological Advancement: Did the process result in a technological advancement, that is to say an advancement in the general understanding? "General understanding" means knowledge available to persons knowledgeable in the field (not a trade secret held privately by a competitor). Importantly, the rejection of a hypothesis or the failure of an experiment still achieves a technological advancement if it generates new technological knowledge explaining why a given approach fails under specific constraints.
Contemporaneous Record-Keeping: Was a detailed record of the hypotheses, tests, and results kept as the work progressed?

2.4 System Uncertainty, Production Runs, and Asset Development Rules

A recurring point of contention in CRA technical reviews involves distinguishing routine engineering from system uncertainty, shop-floor experimental production runs, and commercial asset development.

Recognized in CRA guidance and affirmed by the Tax Court of Canada in 1726437 Ontario Inc. (o/a Airmax Technologies) v. The Queen (2012 TCC 376) and A&D Precision Limited v. The Queen (2019 TCC 48), system uncertainty arises when a claimant integrates known, off-the-shelf technologies or standard engineering components into a novel, tightly constrained system, and the complex interactions among the subsystems create unpredictable physical, mechanical, thermal, acoustic, or computational behaviours that cannot be predicted or resolved using standard engineering principles. When a project faces system-level technological uncertainty—as further illustrated in 6379249 Canada Inc. v. The Queen (2015 TCC 77), where tight geometric and power constraints in a miniature printer created interrelated paper-curling and battery-drain uncertainties—the CRA and the Tax Court evaluate eligibility at the overall system level rather than isolating individual components.

When experimental trials are executed on a commercial manufacturing line, the CRA's SR&ED During Production Runs Policy dictates that labour, material, and incremental overhead costs incurred during the experimental trial run are allowable only to the extent required to test the hypothesis. Any output beyond what is strictly necessary for the experiment constitutes excess production, and all labour, overhead, and material costs attributable to excess or commercial production are disallowed under paragraph 248(1)(i).

Similarly, the CRA's SR&ED while Developing an Asset Policy distinguishes among prototypes, pilot plants, and custom commercial assets. An experimental prototype—an original trial model constructed solely to test a technological hypothesis that has no commercial utility or only nominal scrap value (<10% of cost) after testing—is treated as a current expenditure (labour and materials consumed on Line 320). Non-commercial scale pilot plants constructed to resolve scaling uncertainties before full commercial plant design qualify to the extent of labour and materials consumed or transformed in resolving those uncertainties. Conversely, when SR&ED is performed during the development of a custom product or commercial asset intended for sale or internal production use, the claimant cannot claim the entire cost of constructing the commercial asset and rely on subsequent ITC recapture. Instead, the claimant must partition the project, claiming only the specific subsystem components and labour hours where SR&ED was performed (reporting the physical inputs to those experimental subsystems as materials transformed on Line 325, which remain subject to ITC recapture upon sale or commercial conversion).
3. Federal SR&ED Tax Credit Rates, Thresholds, and Bill C-15 Reforms
3.1 The Legislative Evolution: 2024 Fall Economic Statement, Budget 2025, and Bill C-15

An accurate audit of federal SR&ED claims spanning 2024 through 2026 requires distinguishing between the pre-reform regime, the interim proposals of the December 16, 2024 Fall Economic Statement (FES), and the final enacted provisions of Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1).

On December 16, 2024, the federal 2024 Fall Economic Statement initially proposed raising the annual expenditure limit for the 35% enhanced ITC from $3,000,000 to $4,500,000, raising the prior-year taxable capital phase-out range from $10,000,000–$50,000,000 to $15,000,000– $75,000,000, extending the 35% enhanced rate to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) based on a three-year average gross revenue phase-out of $15,000,000–$75,000,000 (with a matching election for CCPCs), and restoring capital expenditures and lease costs after December 15, 2024. Subsequently, on November 4, 2025, the 2025 Federal Budget (Canada Strong Budget 2025) confirmed all December 2024 FES measures and further increased the annual expenditure limit from the proposed $4,500,000 to $6,000,000, effective retroactively for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024. On March 26, 2026, Bill C-15 received Royal Assent, enacting the complete package—including the $6,000,000 expenditure limit—into law. Consequently, any tax commentary citing $3,000,000 or $4,500,000 as the current expenditure limit for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 is outdated; the enacted statutory limit is $6,000,000, yielding a maximum annual refundable enhanced credit of $2,100,000 on current expenditures (up from $1,050,000 under pre-reform law and $1,575,000 under the interim 2024 FES proposal).

body.text: 3.2 Complete Entity Rate and Refundability Matrix

Under sections 127 and 127.1 of the Income Tax Act, both the ITC rate (35% versus 15%) and the cash refundability percentage (100%, 40%, or 0%) depend on the claimant's precise legal classification throughout the taxation year.

A Canadian-Controlled Private Corporation (CCPC), defined in subsection 125(7) of the Act, is a private corporation that is a Canadian corporation other than one controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever (encompassing both de jure voting control and de facto control under subsection 256(5.1), as examined in McGillivray Restaurant Ltd. v. The Queen, 2016 FCA 99), by one or more non-resident persons, by one or more public corporations (other than a prescribed venture capital corporation), by a corporation with a class of shares listed on a designated stock exchange, or by any combination thereof. Within the CCPC category, the Act further distinguishes between a Qualifying Corporation (subsection 127.1(2))—a CCPC whose prior-year taxable income, combined with all associated corporations, did not exceed its qualifying income limit—and an Excluded Corporation. A Qualifying Corporation (other than an excluded corporation) not only receives 100% refundability on its 35% enhanced ITC for current expenditures (and 40% on capital expenditures) up to its $6,000,000 expenditure limit, but also receives a 40% cash refund on the 15% basic ITC earned on current and capital expenditures exceeding the expenditure limit. Conversely, an Excluded Corporation has its refundability rate capped at 40% across both its 35% enhanced ITCs and its 15% basic ITCs, while a CCPC that is neither a qualifying corporation nor an excluded corporation receives 100% refundability on current 35% ITCs (and 40% on capital 35% ITCs) up to its expenditure limit, but 0% refundability on 15% ITCs over the expenditure limit.

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Bill C-15 introduced the Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC) under subsection 127(9). To qualify as an ECPC throughout a taxation year, a corporation must: (1) be resident in Canada; (2) have a class of shares listed on a designated stock exchange (or have elected or been designated by the Minister of National Revenue to be a public corporation); and (3) not be controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever, by one or more non-resident persons (even if all shares owned by non-residents were owned by a single hypothetical person). In addition, a Canadian-resident corporation in which all or substantially all (≥90%) of the fair market value of all issued shares are owned by one or more ECPCs also qualifies. An ECPC earns the 35% enhanced ITC up to its $6,000,000 expenditure limit (with 100% refundability on current expenditures and 40% refundability on capital expenditures), while expenditures exceeding its expenditure limit earn a non-refundable 15% ITC.

body.text: 3.3 Expenditure Limit Phase-Out Formulas and Group Allocations
3.3.1 CCPC Taxable Capital Phase-Out Formula (Subsections 127(10.2) and (10.21))

For a CCPC that does not elect to use the gross revenue phase-out method, the annual expenditure limit decreases on a straight-line basis once the taxable capital employed in Canada (determined under Part I.3 of the Act, sections 181.2, 181.3, and 181.4) of the corporation and all associated corporations for the immediately preceding taxation year exceeds the lower threshold.
For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024 ($3,000,000 base limit, $10,000,000 to $50,000,000 phase-out):

Expenditure limit = $3,000,000 × ($40,000,000 − A) ÷ $40,000,000, where A is nil if prior-year taxable capital is $10,000,000 or less, and in any other case A is the lesser of $40,000,000 and the amount by which prior-year taxable capital exceeds $10,000,000.
For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 ($6,000,000 base limit, $15,000,000 to $75,000,000 phase-out):

Expenditure limit = $6,000,000 × ($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000, where A is nil if prior-year taxable capital is $15,000,000 or less, and in any other case A is the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which prior-year taxable capital exceeds $15,000,000.

Under this post-December 15, 2024 formula, every $10 of prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada above $15,000,000 reduces the $6,000,000 expenditure limit by $1, reaching $0 (nil) when prior-year taxable capital reaches $75,000,000. Note that while the federal taxable income phase-out was eliminated for taxation years ending after March 18, 2019, Ontario still retains a $500,000 to $800,000 prior-year federal taxable income phase-out for its provincial 8% OITC.
3.3.2 ECPC and Electing CCPC Three-Year Average Gross Revenue Phase-Out (Subsections 127(10.6), (10.31), and (10.32))

Because public corporations and venture-backed technology scale-ups often raise substantial paid-up capital on equity markets that inflates their Part I.3 taxable capital well before achieving commercial revenue scale, subsection 127(10.6) determines an ECPC's $6,000,000 expenditure limit using a three-year average annual gross revenue test:

Expenditure limit = $6,000,000 × ($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000, where A is nil if the average annual revenue for the three fiscal years ending before the taxation year is $15,000,000 or less, and in any other case A is the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which that average exceeds $15,000,000 (so that the limit reaches nil at a three-year average of $75,000,000).

For a standalone ECPC, gross revenue is determined from its annual financial statements prepared in accordance with Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP) and presented to shareholders for the three preceding fiscal years. If an ECPC is a member of a consolidated corporate group that prepares consolidated financial statements, the $6,000,000 expenditure limit must be shared among all group members, and the revenue used is the consolidated annual gross revenue reflected in the group's consolidated financial statements presented to shareholders at the highest level of consolidation for the preceding three fiscal years.

Crucially, under subsections 127(10.31) and 127(10.32), a CCPC may elect on a prescribed form to determine its $6,000,000 expenditure limit using this exact same 3-year average gross revenue phase-out formula instead of the Part I.3 taxable capital formula. When an associated CCPC group makes this election under subsection 127(10.32), the calculation requires summing the average annual revenue reflected in the financial statements of each corporation that is a member of the associated group in the taxation year across the preceding three fiscal years, regardless of whether the corporations were associated during the entirety of that three-year look-back period. This election provides major tax relief to capital-intensive CCPCs (such as biotechnology, semiconductor, clean energy, and hardware ventures) that hold over $15,000,000 in paid-up equity capital or debt from financing rounds while generating under $15,000,000 in gross revenue.
3.3.3 Proration for Short Taxation Years and Associated Group Allocations

If a CCPC or ECPC has a taxation year shorter than 51 weeks (fewer than 357 days), its expenditure limit is prorated by multiplying the calculated limit by the ratio of the number of days in the short taxation year to 365. Special rules under subsection 127(10.5) also apply when a CCPC has more than one taxation year ending in the same calendar year while associated in two or more of those years with another CCPC. Associated CCPCs must file Schedule T2SCH49 (Agreement Among Associated Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit, updated May 29, 2026) to allocate the shared expenditure limit among members; if an associated group fails to file an agreement, the Minister may allocate the limit under subsection 127(10.4). Note that the Income Tax Act includes specific relief rules to prevent unconnected venture capital investors from inadvertently causing portfolio CCPCs to become associated for SR&ED expenditure limit purposes.
3.4 Carryback, Carryforward, Loss Restriction Events, and Assignment of Refundable ITCs

Any non-refundable SR&ED ITC (or refundable ITC that a claimant elects not to have refunded) may be carried back up to 3 preceding taxation years (subsection 127(5)) to recover Part I tax paid in those years, or carried forward up to 20 subsequent taxation years. Any ITC not applied against Part I tax payable within the 20-year carryforward window expires permanently. When an SR&ED ITC is refunded in cash under section 127.1, subsection 127.1(3) deems the refunded amount to have been deducted against Part I tax otherwise payable in the year, thereby reducing the remaining ITC balance available for carryback or carryforward.

When control of a corporation is acquired by a person or group of persons (a loss restriction event), strict streaming rules under subsections 37(6.1), 127(9.1), and 127(9.2) restrict the utilization of both the subsection 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures and unused SR&ED ITC carryforwards. Specifically, pre-acquisition SR&ED expenditure pools and ITC carryforwards can only be deducted or applied in subsequent years if the particular business to which the SR&ED related continues to be carried on by the corporation for profit or with a reasonable expectation of profit, and only to the extent of the corporation's income (or Part I tax payable attributable to income) from that same or a similar business. Parallel restrictions govern the carryback of post-acquisition ITCs to pre-acquisition taxation years. Conversely, where predecessor corporations undergo a qualifying amalgamation (section 87) or wind-up (subsection 88(1)), the successor corporation generally steps into the shoes of the predecessor for SR&ED pool and ITC continuation purposes. Finally, the CRA's SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy (Section 4.5) provides administrative guidelines governing the assignment of a refundable SR&ED investment tax credit (commonly used by startups to secure non-dilutive bridge loans while awaiting refund processing).
4. Qualifying Expenditures (Allowable and Qualified SR&ED Expenditures)

In Canadian SR&ED tax accounting, a strict distinction exists between allowable SR&ED expenditures (computed in Part 3 of Form T661 and added to the subsection 37(1) income deduction pool) and qualified SR&ED expenditures (computed in Part 4 of Form T661 and forming the subsection 127(9) pool on which ITCs are earned).
4.1 Salaries and Wages (In-House Labour)
4.1.1 General Eligibility, Taxable Benefits, and Exclusions (SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy)

Under subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act, "salary or wages" means income of a taxpayer from an office or employment as computed under subdivision a of Division B of Part I (sections 5, 6, and 7 of the Act, generally corresponding to gross employment income reported on a T4 slip). Under the CRA's SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy (updated January 28, 2025), allowable SR&ED salaries and wages include base salaries, hourly wages, overtime pay, regular vacation pay and statutory holiday pay (prorated by the employee's SR&ED time allocation), sick leave taken in the ordinary course of employment, signing bonuses or employment inducements, and bonuses or remuneration based on profits paid to non-specified (arm's-length) employees.

Salary or wages also include expenditures made by the employer in respect of a taxable benefit to an employee under section 6 of the Act (such as automobile benefits, housing/board/meals, group term life insurance policies, tuition fees, or employer contributions to an employee savings plan). While a direct cash outlay for a taxable benefit is includable, a non-cash taxable benefit may be included in SR&ED salary or wages only if three cumulative conditions are satisfied: (1) the value of the benefit is a reasonable estimate of actual costs; (2) the value does not include any GST/HST or PST (unless no input tax credit can be claimed); and (3) the actual costs to which the non-cash benefit relates are not claimed elsewhere as a business expense.
Conversely, five specific categories of compensation and benefit costs are strictly excluded from SR&ED salary or wages on Lines 300–309:

items: Employer's Share of Related Benefits: Employer contributions to the Canada Pension Plan (CPP), Québec Pension Plan (QPP), Employment Insurance (EI), provincial Employer Health Tax (EHT), Workers' Compensation Boards, and employer-paid registered pension plans are not employment income under sections 5–7 and cannot be claimed as SR&ED salary or wages. Under the Traditional Method, the employer's share of related benefits for hands-on SR&ED employees may be claimed on Line 360 as overhead; under the Proxy Method, they are covered by the 55% PPA.

Employee Stock Option Benefits (Section 7 ITA): Benefits deemed received by an employee upon exercising stock options or receiving treasury shares are not cash expenditures incurred by the corporation and are 100% excluded.

Retiring Allowances (Severance): Retiring allowances (including accumulated vacation and sick leave credits paid upon retirement) are excluded from SR&ED salary or wages. However, under the Traditional Method, a retiring allowance paid to a hands-on SR&ED employee (never clerical/administrative staff) may be claimed on Line 360 as overhead based on the employee's historical SR&ED salary ratio over their career.

Extended Vacation or Extended Sick Leave: Remuneration paid during extended leaves of absence is excluded because the employee is neither directly engaged in nor undertaking, supervising, or supporting SR&ED during that period.

Partnership Member Remuneration: Because a partner cannot legally be an employee of a partnership for income tax purposes, any salary or wages paid to a partner is treated as a distribution of partnership income and cannot be claimed as an SR&ED expenditure.

body.text: 4.1.2 "Directly Engaged" (Proxy Method) vs. "Directly Attributable" (Traditional Method)

The scope of claimable employee labour depends on the overhead method elected on Form T661. When electing the Proxy Method, only the portion of salary or wages of employees who are directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada may be claimed on Lines 300–309 and included in the Part 5 PPA salary base. Whether an employee is "directly engaged" is a question of fact determined strictly by the hands-on tasks performed, not by the employee's job title. Qualifying hands-on tasks include preparing equipment and materials for experiments (excluding routine maintenance), carrying out experiments and analyses, recording measurements, performing commensurate paragraph 248(1)(d) support work, and first-line technical supervision. First-line managers and supervisors qualify as directly engaged only for the time spent directly directing the technical course of ongoing SR&ED or performing technological planning for claimed projects (such as assigning technological personnel, setting job priorities, developing technological strategies, or specifying material quality). Non-technological management, administrative decision-making, executive oversight above the first-line level, and clerical/administrative support (payroll, accounting, legal, purchasing, shipping, human resources, maintenance) are not "directly engaged" and are covered instead by the 55% PPA. Under Regulation 2900(5), if a non-specified employee spends all or substantially all (ASA, ≥90%) of their total working time in the year directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada, 100% of their eligible salary or wages for the year is deemed directly engaged.

When using the Traditional Method, in addition to claiming hands-on employees on Lines 300–309, the claimant may claim directly attributable administrative and clerical salaries on Line 360 (Overhead and other expenditures). To qualify on Line 360, the clerical or administrative staff (e.g., human resources, accounting, or purchasing personnel) must provide a non-technological service that aids ongoing SR&ED, and the wage portion claimed must satisfy both the directly related test (a direct linkage with no intervening step to the SR&ED work, SR&ED staff, or SR&ED equipment—for example, a Personnel Manager's time spent hiring an SR&ED engineer qualifies, whereas a Vice-President's time hiring that Personnel Manager does not) and the incremental test (would not have been incurred if the SR&ED had not occurred).
4.1.3 Specified Employees: Statutory Definition and Three-Tier Cap Architecture

Under subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act, a "specified employee" of a taxpayer is an employee who either: (1) is a specified shareholder of the corporation (an individual who owns, directly or indirectly at any time in the year, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or of any related corporation); or (2) does not deal at arm's length with the employer (such as a spouse, child, parent, or sibling of a controlling shareholder under section 251).

Because owner-managers can control how corporate profits are distributed between dividends and salaries, the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations impose three distinct statutory restrictions on specified employees (reported on Line 305 for work in Canada and Line 309 for work outside Canada):

items: Absolute Prohibition on Bonuses and Profit-Based Remuneration (Paragraph 37(9)(a) ITA): Any bonus or remuneration based on profits paid to a specified employee is 100% excluded from allowable SR&ED expenditures under both the Traditional and Proxy Methods.

Direct SR&ED Salary Expenditure Cap of 5 × YMPE (Subsection 37(9.1) ITA): The maximum amount of base salary or wages paid to a specified employee that can be claimed as a direct SR&ED expenditure on Line 305/309 for a taxation year is capped at 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined under the Canada Pension Plan for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days in the taxation year on which the individual is a specified employee of the taxpayer (divided by 365). Per Canadian CPA tax guidance for 2026, the CPP YMPE is $74,600, establishing a maximum direct SR&ED salary deduction cap of $373,000 (5 × $74,600) per specified employee (shared across associated corporations).

Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Salary Base Cap (Subsections 2900(7) and 2900(8) ITR): When calculating the eligible salary base in Part 5 of Form T661 for the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount, the amount included for each specified employee (Line 860) is restricted to the lesser of three amounts: (a) Actual SR&ED Salary (Line 856), equal to the specified employee's total base salary or wages for the year (excluding bonuses, profit-based pay, taxable benefits, and prior-year unpaid wages paid in the year) multiplied by the percentage of time spent directly engaged in SR&ED (up to 100%); (b) The 75% Total Salary Ceiling, equal to 75% of the specified employee's total base salary or wages for the year across both SR&ED and non-SR&ED work (excluding bonuses, profit-based pay, taxable benefits, and prior-year unpaid wages); or (c) The 2.5 × YMPE Ceiling (Line 858), equal to 2.5 × YMPE × (days employed in tax year ÷ 365) (with no proration for days the employee was not a specified employee). For 2026 (YMPE = $74,600), this PPA salary base ceiling is $186,500 (2.5 × $74,600). Under subsection 2900(8) ITR, if a specified employee is employed by two or more associated corporations, the single 2.5 × YMPE ($186,500) ceiling must be allocated among the associated corporations using Form T1174 (Agreement Between Associated Corporations to Allocate Salary or Wages of Specified Employees for SR&ED).

body.text: 4.1.4 The 180-Day Unpaid Remuneration Rule (Subsection 78(4) ITA)

Under subsection 78(4) of the Income Tax Act, any salary, wages, or other remuneration accrued in a taxation year that remains unpaid on the day that is 180 days after the end of the taxation year is deemed not to have been incurred in that taxation year. Instead, it must be subtracted on Line 315 of Form T661 for the year accrued and is deemed to be an expenditure incurred in the subsequent taxation year in which it is actually paid (claimed on Line 310). However, under Regulation 2900(9) and the CRA's Prescribed Proxy Amount Policy, prior-year unpaid salary or wages claimed on Line 310 in the year paid are permanently excluded from the PPA salary base; thus, failure to pay accrued SR&ED salaries within 180 days of year-end results in a permanent forfeiture of the 55% PPA on those wages.
4.1.5 Permissible Foreign SR&ED Salaries and Wages (Subsections 37(1.4), 37(1.5), and 37(9)(b) ITA)

While SR&ED must generally be carried on in Canada (including Canada's Exclusive Economic Zone under subsection 37(1.3)), subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5) allow a taxpayer to claim permissible salary or wages for SR&ED performed outside Canada (reported on Line 307 for non-specified employees and Line 309 for specified employees) if five cumulative statutory criteria are met: (1) the work is performed directly by an employee of the claimant (never a subcontractor or consultant); (2) the employee was a resident of Canada at the time the expense was incurred; (3) the work is related to a business of the claimant; (4) the work performed outside Canada is an integral part of, and solely in support of, an SR&ED project carried on in Canada directly by the claimant; and (5) the claimant reasonably believes that the salary or wages are not subject to an income or profits tax imposed by a foreign country (paragraph 37(9)(b)). Under subsection 37(1.5), the maximum permissible foreign SR&ED salary or wages claimable in a taxation year is capped at the lesser of: (a) actual qualifying foreign SR&ED salaries/wages incurred in the year; and (b) 10% of the total eligible Canadian SR&ED salaries and wages (Lines 300 + 305) directly undertaken by the claimant in the year. Any foreign R&D expenses exceeding this 10% cap (or incurred via foreign contractors) may be deducted directly against business income under subsection 37(2), but cannot enter the subsection 37(1) pool or earn ITCs.
4.2 Materials Consumed vs. Materials Transformed (Materials for SR&ED Policy)

Under clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A) (Traditional Method), subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V) (Proxy Method), and paragraph 2900(2)(a) of the Income Tax Regulations, a claimant may claim the cost of materials under either overhead method in two distinct categories: Materials Consumed in the Prosecution of SR&ED (Line 320) and Materials Transformed in the Prosecution of SR&ED (Line 325). Under the CRA's Materials for SR&ED Policy, an item qualifies as a "material for SR&ED" only if it satisfies the "Body of a Thing" Test: the raw materials, substances, or other items must be physical and tangible (in a solid, liquid, or gaseous state) and must, at a given moment in the SR&ED process, compose the body of a tangible object ("thing") on which the SR&ED is being carried out, or compose the body of a tangible object that results from the SR&ED. body.text: 4.3 Subcontractors (SR&ED Contracts) and Third-Party Payments
4.3.1 Arm's-Length vs. Non-Arm's Length SR&ED Contracts (Contract Expenditures for SR&ED Performed on Behalf of a Claimant Policy)

When a claimant contracts another person or partnership to perform SR&ED in Canada on behalf of the claimant (subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01)), the tax treatment diverges sharply depending on whether the contractor deals at arm's length with the claimant.

For Arm's-Length SR&ED Contracts (Line 340), the work must constitute basic research, applied research, experimental development, or eligible paragraph 248(1)(d) support work (commensurate with needs and directly in support of the payer's SR&ED) performed in Canada on behalf of the claimant by a taxable supplier. While 100% of the eligible arm's-length contract expenditure is added to the subsection 37(1) deductible pool on Line 340, subparagraph (a)(ii) of the definition of "qualified expenditure" in subsection 127(9) restricts the amount included in qualified expenditures for ITC calculation purposes to 80% of the contract expenditure (with the 20% reduction subtracted on Line 529 of Form T661). To prevent duplication of ITC entitlement, an arm's-length contractor performing basic research, applied research, or experimental development may file its own SR&ED claim, but must reduce its qualified expenditures dollar-for-dollar by the contract payment received or receivable from the Canadian payer under subsection 127(18) (note that a contractor hired solely for paragraph 248(1)(d) support work cannot claim SR&ED in its own right unless it deals at non-arm's length with the payer). Payments for contracted SR&ED work not yet performed by year-end are disallowed as prepaid expenses under subsection 18(9) until the year the work is performed. Furthermore, accrued contract amounts unpaid 180 days after year-end are excluded from qualified expenditures under subsection 127(26) (Line 520); when paid in a later year, 80% of the amount paid is added back on Line 500, provided the unpaid expenditure was identified on Form T661 within the original 18-month reporting deadline. Finally, following the restoration of capital expenditures under Bill C-15, contract expenditures and third-party payments incurred after December 15, 2024 are generally no longer reduced under the subsection 37(14) look-through rule for capital or equipment lease expenditures of the performer (except for excluded building costs).

For Non-Arm's Length (NAL) SR&ED Contracts (Line 345), where a claimant contracts a related or non-arm's length party (section 251) to perform SR&ED on its behalf, 100% of the contract payment is deductible by the payer in its subsection 37(1) pool (Line 345), but 0% is a qualified expenditure for the payer's ITC calculation (subtracted on Line 541 pursuant to paragraph (f) of "qualified expenditure" in subsection 127(9)). Instead, the amount received by the NAL performer is not considered a "contract payment" under subsection 127(9), allowing the NAL performer to claim its own underlying SR&ED salaries, materials, and PPA without reduction. Alternatively, under subsection 127(13), the NAL performer and NAL payer may jointly file Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length, updated May 15, 2026) to transfer all or part of the performer's qualified expenditures (capped at the lesser of the performer's otherwise qualified expenditures and the contract amount) to the payer (reported on Line 508 / Line 510 by the transferee and deducted on Line 544 / Line 546 by the transferor). Because a partnership is not a "person" for subsection 127(13) purposes, a partnership can never transfer or receive qualified expenditures on Form T1146. Under subsection 127(24), anti-avoidance rules invalidate arrangements that interpose an arm's-length intermediary between two NAL parties for the main purpose of obtaining qualified expenditures.
4.3.2 Third-Party Payments (Line 370, Form T1263 — Third-Party Payments Policy)

Under subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.1), (ii), and (iii), a claimant may claim third-party payments (reported on Line 370, with a separate Form T1263 attached for each payment) made to six statutory categories of entities ("A" through "F" Entities: Canadian-resident corporations, approved associations, approved universities/colleges/research institutes, non-profit R&D corporations exempt under paragraph 149(1)(j), and approved granting councils) to be used for SR&ED carried on in Canada related to a business of the claimant, provided the claimant is entitled to exploit the results of the SR&ED. Like arm's-length contracts, 80% of an eligible third-party payment is included in qualified expenditures for ITC purposes (20% subtracted on Line 529). body.text: 4.4 Overhead Expenditures: The Proxy Method vs. Traditional Method Election
4.4.1 The Irrevocable Annual Election and the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA)

In Part 3, Section A of Form T661, a claimant must choose between two mutually exclusive methods for handling SR&ED overhead and indirect support costs for the taxation year. Under the Proxy Method (Line 160), the claimant elects pursuant to subsection 37(10) ITA to compute a notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) in Part 5 of Form T661 (reported on Line 502) in lieu of specifically tracking and claiming actual SR&ED overhead expenditures. Under subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations, the PPA rate is 55% of the eligible salary base (the rate was 65% for 2012 and prior years, 60% prorated for 2013, and has been fixed at 55% since January 1, 2014). Crucially, the PPA is a notional amount that is added only to qualified SR&ED expenditures (Part 4) to earn ITCs; the PPA is not added to the subsection 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures (instead, the underlying actual overhead expenses remain deductible as ordinary business expenses under section 9 of the Act).

Under the Traditional Method (Line 162), the claimant identifies, tracks, allocates, and substantiates actual overhead and other expenditures on Line 360 that are directly related and incremental to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada (subsections 2900(2)(c) and 2900(3)(b) ITR). Actual overhead claimed on Line 360 is added to both the subsection 37(1) deductible pool and the subsection 127(9) qualified expenditure pool. Under subsection 37(10) ITA, the election between the Proxy Method and Traditional Method is made on a year-by-year basis when Form T661 is first filed for the taxation year and is strictly irrevocable for that year once filed (if neither box is ticked, the CRA processes the claim using the Traditional Method). Furthermore, under subsection 2900(6) ITR, the PPA is subject to an Overall Cap equal to A − B − C, where A is total business deductions for tax purposes (including cost of goods sold), B is specified statutory deductions (such as CCA under s. 20(1)(a), the s. 37(1) SR&ED deduction, interest under s. 20(1)(c), and resource deductions), and C is building rent/occupancy expenses.
4.4.2 Treatment of Cloud Computing (AWS, Azure, GCP) and Software Licences

A critical audit issue for modern software, artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), and data analytics claimants is the eligibility of cloud computing infrastructure (such as AWS EC2/S3, Microsoft Azure, or Google Cloud Platform GPU training clusters) and software subscriptions/licences. Because cloud compute cycles, SaaS subscriptions, and digital datasets are intangible services or rights of use rather than physical, tangible substances composing the "body of a thing," they never qualify as SR&ED materials on Lines 320 or 325. Under the Proxy Method, all overhead and indirect infrastructure costs are covered by the 55% PPA; consequently, cloud computing bills and software subscriptions cannot be claimed separately when electing the Proxy Method.

Conversely, as highlighted in Canadian CPA advisory guidance, under the Traditional Method, cloud computing costs and specialized software tools may be claimed on Line 360 as overhead and other expenditures if and only if the claimant proves with contemporaneous resource-tagged billing logs that the costs satisfy both the directly related test and the incremental test (for example, dedicated cloud GPU clusters spun up specifically for a series of ML training experiments, billed separately, and shut down afterward, which would not have been incurred had the SR&ED not occurred). Standing production hosting environments, multi-tenant customer servers, fixed monthly internet/telephone plans (other than identifiable incremental long-distance charges), and general corporate software licences fail the incremental test and are disallowed. Moreover, even under the Traditional Method, expenditures listed in section 2902 of the Income Tax Regulations—including fees paid to prepare SR&ED claims, legal and accounting fees, general administration, headhunter/recruiting fees and hiring advertising (note: employee relocation moving expenses within Canada can qualify under the Traditional Method), interest expenses (Reg. 2902(a)(i)(C)), and costs to attend conventions or conferences (Reg. 2902(a)(i)(F))—are prescribed expenditures that are excluded from earning ITCs.

body.text: 4.5 Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), and Equipment Lease Costs (Post-December 15, 2024 Restoration)

Following the enactment of Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026 and the publication of the updated SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (June 29, 2026), SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (June 8 / June 22, 2026), and SR&ED Shared-Use-Equipment Policy (May 22, 2026), capital property and leased equipment have been restored to the SR&ED program for property acquired (and available for use) or lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024.

For SR&ED Capital Expenditures (Paragraph 37(1)(b) ITA — Lines 380 & 390, Box 782), eligibility applies to depreciable property (other than land, a leasehold interest in land, a building, or a leasehold interest in a building, unless it is a prescribed special-purpose building approved by the Department of Finance Canada under Regulation 2903; portable shelters and non-building structures are not restricted by the building exclusion) acquired and available for use (subsection 37(1.2)) after December 15, 2024. At the time of acquisition, the claimant must intend either: (a) to use the property during all or substantially all (ASA, ≥90%) of its operating time over its expected useful life in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada; or (b) to consume ASA (≥90%) of its value in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. Both new and used ASA depreciable property qualify for the 100% immediate income deduction in the subsection 37(1) pool (deemed CCA under subsection 37(6)). However, under paragraph 2902(b) ITR, used equipment (entered on Line 390 and subtracted on Line 532) is a prescribed expenditure that does NOT qualify for SR&ED ITCs; only new ASA capital property earns ITCs. Furthermore, under the Proxy Method, General-Purpose Office Equipment or Furniture (GPOEF — desks, chairs, lamps, filing cabinets, photocopiers, fax machines, telephones) cannot be claimed as an SR&ED capital expenditure because it is covered by the PPA. For a CCPC or ECPC earning the 35% enhanced ITC on new ASA capital property within its $6,000,000 expenditure limit, the capital ITC is 40% refundable in cash (an effective 14.0% cash refund, with the remaining 21.0% available to offset Part I tax payable or carry back 3 / forward 20 years).

For Shared-Use Equipment (SUE — Subsection 127(9) ITA — Line 504, Box 792), eligibility applies to new depreciable property acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024 that does not meet the ≥90% ASA test, is not GPOEF, and is not Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP) under Regulation 2900(11) (property intended at acquisition to be used for SR&ED during the assembly, construction, or commissioning of a commercial manufacturing facility or plant and thereafter used primarily for non-SR&ED commercial purposes). If the equipment is actually used primarily (>50% but <90% of its total operating time) for SR&ED in Canada during the First Period (starting when available for use and ending at the end of the first taxation year that ends at least 12 months after that date), 25% (1/4) of its capital cost (excluding borrowing costs under s. 21 and adjusted for NAL transfers under s. 127(11.6)) is included as a qualified expenditure on Line 504 for ITC purposes. If it continues to be used primarily (>50%) for SR&ED during the Second Period (starting when available for use and ending at the end of the first taxation year that ends at least 24 months after that date), an additional 25% (1/4) of its capital cost is included on Line 504 in that second year (for a cumulative maximum of 50% of capital cost). SUE capital cost does not enter the subsection 37(1) pool; it is depreciated on Schedule T2SCH8 under normal CCA rules (with any SUE ITC claimed reducing the Undepreciated Capital Cost [UCC] of the class in the following year).

For Equipment Lease Costs (Lines 350, 355, and 360, Box 759), eligibility applies to lease costs first becoming payable after December 15, 2024 for equipment used in SR&ED in Canada (building rent remains strictly excluded under both methods unless it is a prescribed special-purpose building; land lease costs may qualify under the Traditional Method if ASA or directly attributable, but are excluded under the Proxy Method). If leased equipment is used ≥90% (ASA) of its operating time for SR&ED, 100% of the lease cost is claimed on Line 350 under both the Traditional and Proxy Methods (excluding GPOEF under Proxy). If leased equipment is used >50% to <90% (Primarily) for SR&ED, under the Proxy Method 50% (one-half) of the lease cost is claimed on Line 355 (excluding GPOEF), whereas under the Traditional Method the actual SR&ED usage percentage is claimed on Line 360 as overhead if directly related and incremental. If leased equipment is used ≤50% for SR&ED, 0% is claimable under the Proxy Method, while the actual SR&ED usage percentage is claimable on Line 360 under the Traditional Method if directly related and incremental. Because eligible equipment lease costs are current expenditures under paragraph 37(1)(a), the 35% enhanced ITC earned on them by a CCPC or ECPC is 100% refundable.
4.6 Government Assistance, Non-Government Assistance, Contract Payments, and Recapture

Under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(18) of the Income Tax Act (and the CRA's Assistance and Contract Payments Policy), a claimant must reduce its subsection 37(1) pool (Lines 429–432) and its qualified expenditures (Lines 513–518) by all government assistance (grants, subsidies, forgivable loans, conditional royalty-repayable contributions, super-allowance benefits, and provincial/territorial R&D tax credits), non-government assistance (inducements or reimbursements included under paragraph 12(1)(x)), and contract payments that the claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive on or before the income tax return filing-due date for the taxation year. Direct wage or project grants—such as funding from the National Research Council Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP), the Strategic Innovation Fund (SIF), or prior-year Canada Emergency Wage Subsidy (CEWS) amounts—reduce eligible SR&ED expenditures dollar-for-dollar, but under the Proxy Method, the claimant still calculates the 55% PPA on the unreduced gross SR&ED salary base before subtracting the government grant in Part 4, preserving significant net SR&ED credits ("stacking"). Moreover, effective for loans made after December 31, 2019, unconditional repayable government loans that meet the statutory definition of an "excluded loan" in subsection 12(11) do not constitute government assistance. When previously deducted assistance is repaid in a subsequent year, it is added back to the subsection 37(1) pool (Line 445) and earns an ITC (Line 560) at the exact ITC rate that applied in the year the assistance originally reduced the claim. Excess assistance within a related group can be allocated among group members using Form T1145.

Under subsections 127(27) to 127(36) of the Income Tax Act (and the CRA's Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy), if a claimant disposes of or converts to commercial use any property—including ASA capital equipment, Shared-Use Equipment, materials transformed (Line 325), or physical property acquired under an arm's-length SR&ED contract—within 20 taxation years of acquiring the property and earning an SR&ED ITC on it, the claimant must add a recapture amount directly to its Part I tax payable (reported on Schedule T2SCH31 / Form T2038(IND)). The recapture amount equals the lesser of: (1) the actual SR&ED ITC originally earned on the property; and (2) the applicable ITC percentage multiplied by the proceeds of disposition (if sold at arm's length) or the fair market value (FMV) of the property at the time of conversion to commercial use or non-arm's length disposition. If an SR&ED performer transferred qualified expenditures to a non-arm's length payer via Form T1146 (subsection 127(13)), subsection 127(29) triggers recapture in the hands of the SR&ED performer (allocating taxpayer) if the underlying property is later sold or converted to commercial use (though disposing of SR&ED capital property to a NAL purchaser who continues to use it ASA for SR&ED does not trigger recapture under subsection 127(33)). Any ITC recaptured in a taxation year is added back to the subsection 37(1) deductible pool in the subsequent taxation year under paragraph 37(1)(c.2) (Line 453). Crucially, materials consumed, salaries, overhead, intellectual property sales, and scrap sales where proceeds/FMV are <10% of cost do not trigger ITC recapture.
5. Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes

Nearly all Canadian provinces and Yukon provide statutory R&D tax credits that stack on top of the federal SR&ED program. Because provincial R&D tax credits constitute government assistance under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(18) of the federal Income Tax Act, provincial credits are computed first and deducted from the federal qualified expenditure base (except for Newfoundland and Labrador's internal provincial calculation and the portion of provincial credits attributable to the notional PPA under the Proxy Method, which is included in income under paragraph 12(1)(x) in the year received rather than reducing the s. 37(1) pool).

5.2.1 Quebec's Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC)

For taxation years or fiscal periods beginning after March 25, 2025, the Government of Quebec enacted a sweeping restructuring of its innovation tax system (detailed in Quebec Finance Information Bulletin 2025-6), abolishing eight legacy tax measures—the tax credit for salaries and wages (R&D) (which formerly paid 14% basic or 30% enhanced on up to $3,000,000 for taxation years beginning on or before March 25, 2025), the tax credit for university research or public research centres, the tax credit for research consortium fees, the tax credit for private partnership pre-competitive research, the tax credit for technological adaptation services, the industrial design component of the design tax credit, and the tax holiday for foreign researchers and experts—and replacing them with the unified Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC — Crédit d'impôt pour la recherche, l'innovation et la commercialisation).

While Quebec's R&D definition remains harmonized with federal subsection 248(1) (and the CRA continues to perform the scientific review of R&D work), the CRIC also covers eligible pre-commercialization activities carried out in Quebec in conjunction with R&D work performed in Quebec by or on behalf of the corporation. Eligible pre-commercialization work encompasses: (1) tests, technological validations, and studies conducted to meet regulatory requirements aimed at obtaining an initial approval or certification for commercializing an innovation (including quality control activities only if they directly relate to implementing a quality control system required for initial regulatory approval or certification); and (2) product design work, including the development of form and aesthetics, improved functionality, and choice of materials.

Under the CRIC, qualified expenditures incurred in Quebec comprise four categories: (1) 100% of salaries and wages paid to the corporation's employees for eligible R&D and pre-commercialization activities; (2) 50% of amounts paid to a subcontractor for an eligible contract carried out in Quebec; (3) 50% of payments made to an eligible Quebec public research centre, research consortium, or university entity; and (4) 100% of property acquisition costs (capital expenditures / CAPEX) for eligible activities in Quebec, excluding land, buildings, or rights to use land or buildings (and excluding property claimed under the C3i investment tax credit or a Large Investment Project tax holiday). Only qualified expenditures exceeding the corporation's annual exclusion threshold earn the CRIC. The exclusion threshold equals the greater of: (a) $50,000; or (b) the sum of the basic personal amount of the applicable personal income tax system (cited as $18,571 per employee in practitioner guidance) for each eligible employee, adjusted for the percentage of time spent by each employee on eligible R&D and pre-commercialization activities. Above this exclusion threshold, the CRIC pays a 30% fully refundable tax credit on the first $1,000,000 of qualified expenditures, and 20% fully refundable on all qualified expenditures exceeding $1,000,000 (claimed on Form RD-1029.8.CR-T).

To illustrate how the Quebec CRIC stacks with the federal SR&ED credit (as modelled by R&D Tax Academy), consider a Quebec CCPC in its 2026 taxation year that pays $1,200,000 in salaries for R&D carried out in Quebec and $200,000 to a Quebec subcontractor, with an applicable exclusion threshold of $100,000, and whose pre-assistance federal qualified expenditures (including the 55% PPA and 80% of the subcontractor) are $2,000,000. If Form T661 or Schedule T2SCH31 / Form T2038(IND) is filed even one day past the 18-month deadline, or if the prescribed project descriptions (Lines 242, 244, 246) or financial lines are left blank at the deadline, the expenditures are permanently barred from SR&ED treatment and all ITCs are forfeited (Westsource Group Holdings Inc. v. The Queen, 2018 FCA 57). Furthermore, if Form T661 is filed on time but Schedule T2SCH31 is filed after the 18-month deadline, the taxpayer may deduct the expenditures in its subsection 37(1) pool but permanently forfeits 100% of the Investment Tax Credits (Easy Way Cattle Oilers Ltd. v. The Queen, 2016 FCA 301).
6.3 The CRA Pre-Claim Approval Process (Launched April 1, 2026) and Advisory Services

To provide upfront technical certainty and accelerate refund processing for small and medium-sized enterprises, the Canada Strong Budget 2025 introduced—and the CRA officially launched on April 1, 2026—the optional SR&ED Pre-Claim Approval Process. Pre-claim approval is available to businesses that: (a) are Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs), Canadian corporations, or Canadian partnerships; (b) have an annual gross income of less than $25,000,000; and (c) are in good compliance standing with the CRA. Eligible businesses apply through a streamlined four-step workflow:

items: Step 1 (Open a Request via Web Form): The business completes an online request form (taking less than five minutes) and receives a CRA case number within 2 to 5 business days.

Step 2 (Submit Application in My Business Account): Using its case number, the business completes its application in the CRA My Business Account portal in a few hours using existing project documentation, requesting pre-claim approval for up to 3 projects before starting work or incurring costs.

Step 3 (Meet with a CRA SR&ED Specialist within 4 Weeks): Within 4 weeks of submitting the application, the claimant meets with a CRA SR&ED specialist (this meeting is mandatory for new SR&ED claimants and scheduled as needed for returning claimants in good standing).

Step 4 (Receive Official Determination within 8 Weeks): Within 8 weeks of completing the application in My Business Account, the CRA issues an official pre-claim approval determination that remains valid for up to 3 years. When the tax return and Form T661 are subsequently filed, if a pre-approved project requires an expenditure-only review, the CRA processing service standard is cut in half from 180 calendar days to 90 calendar days.

body.text: In addition to Pre-Claim Approval, the CRA operates the First-Time Claimant Advisory Service (FTCAS) (launched January 1, 2014 to provide educational guidance to first-time filers), the online Self-Assessment and Learning Tool (SALT), monthly informational webinars, and one-on-one outreach consultations via OESCPB-SVEDGPO@cra-arc.gc.ca.
