6.4.2 Coordinated RTA/FR Review Process, Proposal Package, and Dispute Resolution

When a filed SR&ED claim is selected for detailed review, it is governed by the CRA's Claim Review Manual for Research and Technology Advisors, Financial Claim Review Manual – Review Procedures for Financial Reviewers, and The SR&ED Review Process: A Guide for Claimants (updated April 20 / July 2, 2025–2026). Every detailed review is coordinated between a Research and Technology Advisor (RTA)—who evaluates whether the claimed work meets subsection 248(1) and reports to a Research and Technology Manager (RTM)—and a Financial Reviewer (FR)—who verifies allowable and qualified expenditures and ITCs under sections 37 and 127 and reports to a Financial Review Manager (FRM). The CRA conducts the majority of reviews virtually via videoconferencing (including virtual facility/laboratory tours), though claimants may request an on-site visit on an exceptional basis subject to management approval. Under sections 230(1) and 231.1 of the Income Tax Act (and judicial precedents such as Ludco Enterprises Ltd. v. MNR, 93 DTC 1351, The Queen v. McKinley Transport Ltd., 90 DTC 6243, and AGT Ltd. v. Canada, 97 DTC 5189), reviewers have statutory authority to inspect books, records, and property and to expand the scope of a review based on risk evaluations, while being strictly prohibited from negotiating eligibility or trading project approvals.

If adjustments are proposed, the CRA sends the claimant a joint Proposal Package containing the RTA's SR&ED Project Eligibility Report, a proposal letter summarizing proposed expenditure and ITC adjustments (and any proposed penalty), and supporting financial details (documented internally in the FR's 10-section Financial Review Report [FRR]). The claimant generally has 30 calendar days from the date of the proposal letter to submit written representations and additional evidence. If concerns remain unresolved, the claimant follows a four-step dispute resolution hierarchy:

items: Step 1 (Reviewer Resolution): Discuss concerns directly with the RTA and FR and submit written representations within the 30-day window.
Step 2 (Manager Escalation): Escalate unresolved technical or financial concerns to the RTM and FRM.

Step 3 (Administrative Review): Request an Administrative Review after receiving the Proposal Package. An Administrative Review is not a second technical review by different reviewers; its sole purpose is to verify that the review complied with SR&ED legislation, policies, and procedures and that the claimant received due process.

Step 4 (Formal Notice of Objection & Tax Court Appeal): Within 90 calendar days from the date the Notice of Assessment or Reassessment is sent (paragraph 165(1)(b) ITA), serve a formal Notice of Objection to the CRA Appeals Branch (noting that the Minister and the Tax Court lack jurisdiction to grant an extension of time unless requested within 1 year and 90 days of the mailing date under subsections 166.1(7) and 166.2(5)), followed by an appeal to the Tax Court of Canada.

body.text: 6.4.3 Statutory Penalties: Claim Preparer Penalty (s. 162(5.1)), Gross Negligence (s. 163(2)), and Criminal Fraud (s. 239(1.1))

Part 9 of Form T661 requires mandatory disclosure of all third-party claim preparers, their Business Numbers, and their fee arrangements (if no preparer assisted, only Lines 935, 970, and 975 are completed). While incomplete or missing Part 9 information does not disallow the SR&ED claim itself, subsection 162(5.1) of the Income Tax Act imposes a $1,000 penalty for which the claimant and the claim preparer are jointly and severally liable.

Under the CRA's Gross Negligence Penalty on Overstated SR&ED Claims Policy (updated January 28, 2025) and subsection 163(2) of the Income Tax Act, if the CRA discharges its burden of proof under subsection 163(3) to establish on a balance of probabilities that a claimant knowingly, or under circumstances amounting to gross negligence (more than a simple error or misunderstanding of the Act), made a false statement or omission in an initial or amended SR&ED claim, the penalty equals the greater of $100 or 50% of the total of: (a) the understated Part I tax payable reasonably attributable to the false statement or omission (paragraph 163(2)(a)); plus (b) the refund of the overstated refundable ITC claimed (paragraph 163(2)(d)). Furthermore, claimants and preparers who fabricate invoices or falsify records face criminal prosecution under paragraphs 239(1.1)(a) and (c) of the Income Tax Act, which mandate summary conviction fines of 50% to 200% of the excess credit or refund claimed (even if the CRA detects the fraud before paying out a refund) in addition to potential imprisonment.
7. Landmark Judicial Precedents and Case Law Analysis

Canadian tax courts have produced a comprehensive body of jurisprudence interpreting every facet of the SR&ED regime. Table 7.1 synthesizes the landmark decisions of the Tax Court of Canada (TCC), the Federal Court of Appeal (FCA), and the Court of Quebec that govern current SR&ED audits and litigation.

cells: Established that SR&ED requires a structured, methodical experimental investigation with documented test parameters and results; unrecorded shop-floor trial-and-error troubleshooting does not qualify.
Highland Foundry Ltd. v. The Queen, [1994] TCJ No. 809 (Docket 92-264)
Timing of the "All or Substantially All" (ASA) test for prototypes & capital property

Held that whether a prototype or capital asset (a patented green-sand foundry refiner) is ASA attributable to SR&ED must be determined based on the taxpayer's intention at the time the expenditures are incurred, not retroactively penalized via hindsight when the successful prototype is later used in commercial production.
CCLC Technologies Inc. v. Canada, 96 DTC 6527, [1996] FCJ No. 1226
Government assistance vs. ordinary business investment (ss. 12(1)(x) & 127(9))

Held that provincial funding under a Coal Research Agreement where the government received no net commercial profit on success and only an equity interest in uncommercial technology on failure was not an ordinary commercial investment, but constituted government assistance reducing qualified SR&ED expenditures.
Established that Parliament enacted the SR&ED regime to encourage scientific research in Canada, and courts should interpret the provisions in light of that legislative purpose.
Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1839, [1998] 3 CTC 2520
The canonical 5-part legal test for SR&ED eligibility under s. 248(1)

Judge Bowman (later Chief Justice of the Tax Court of Canada) articulated the five foundational criteria: (1) technological risk/uncertainty beyond routine engineering; (2) formulation of hypotheses (5-stage process); (3) adherence to the scientific method; (4) technological advancement in general understanding (including failed experiments); and (5) keeping detailed contemporaneous records as work progresses.
RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen, 99 DTC 5087, [1998] FCJ No. 1890
Rejection of rigid "third-party repeatability" documentary threshold

Reversed the Tax Court; Robertson J.A. held that while contemporaneous documentation is the primary way to prove systematic research, where credible evidence establishes that testing occurred and actually resulted in a patented technological advancement (a spatial membrane concrete panel), a strong inference of systematic research arises even if raw test logs were unavailable due to the engineer's death.
C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393 (aff'g 2000 DTC 2372)
Appellate adoption of Northwest Hydraulic in custom software development

Formally adopted the 5 Northwest Hydraulic criteria at the FCA level; held that building a complex custom lottery software system (IDLS) using standard programming techniques without resolving technological uncertainty is routine engineering, and affirmed drawing an adverse inference when the claimant fails to call hands-on project managers to testify.
1373744 Ontario Inc. (o/a One Source Metal) v. The Queen, 2009 TCC 511
Burden of proving timely filing of technical project narratives (s. 37(11))

Dismissed the appeal where the claimant's T661 forms were date-stamped received prior to the 18-month deadline, but the accompanying technical project report lacked a stamp and was faxed 12 days after the statutory deadline.
Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen, 2011 FCA 355 (aff'g 2010 TCC 319)
Routine engineering vs. technological uncertainty in product design

Affirmed that testing standard materials (plastics vs. aluminum) to design a lighter, higher-capacity storage bin system using techniques accessible to competent professionals is routine engineering, not SR&ED.
Murray Arlin Dentistry PC v. The Queen, 2012 TCC 133
Substantiation of applied research hours vs. automated software output

Dismissed a periodontist's claim for tracking dental implant outcomes in commercial software; held that generating automated comparative tables and estimating 20% of salary without contemporaneous time logs failed to substantiate systematic applied research in the tax years.
1726437 Ontario Inc. (o/a Airmax Technologies) v. The Queen, 2012 TCC 376
Recognition of "system uncertainty" in component integration

Allowed the taxpayer's claim for developing a compact, low-noise (40 dB) high-static-pressure residential HVAC system; confirmed that integrating modified off-the-shelf components where subsystem interactions create unpredictable acoustic and pressure behaviours constitutes qualifying system uncertainty (though recovery was capped at $12,000 per year due to the Informal Procedure limit in s. 18.1 of the Tax Court of Canada Act).
Fio Corporation v. The Queen, 2014 TCC 58 (aff'd 2015 FCA)
Implied undertaking rule in SR&ED Tax Court discovery

Held that the CRA breached the implied undertaking rule by using 260 documents obtained during pre-trial discovery in a 2007–2008 SR&ED appeal to issue new reassessments; barred the Crown from using discovery documents in separate proceedings without leave of the Court and awarded $25,000 costs.
Les Abeilles Service de Conditionnement Inc. v. The Queen, 2014 TCC 313
Contemporaneous documentation is not a strict legal sine qua non

Justice Jorré allowed four assembly-line experimental development projects, holding that while contemporaneous records are strongly recommended, their absence is not a fatal legal bar (sine qua non) if credible testimony and corroborating evidence establish all five Northwest Hydraulic criteria.
6379249 Canada Inc. v. The Queen, 2015 TCC 77
Persistence of system-level technological uncertainty after failed commercial release

Justice D'Auray vacated CRA reassessments and allowed 2009–2010 SR&ED claims for a miniature wireless portable printer; held that releasing 200 defective units that failed in the field (paper curling and battery drain) and were recalled from the market did not terminate SR&ED eligibility while severe system-level technological uncertainties remained unresolved.
Easy Way Cattle Oilers Ltd. v. The Queen, 2016 FCA 301 (aff'g 2015 TCC 211)
Strict enforcement of the 18-month deadline for Schedule T2SCH31 (s. 127(9)(m))

Unanimously held that filing Form T661 and the T2 return on time, but filing Schedule T2SCH31 47 days past the 18-month statutory deadline, permanently barred the taxpayer from claiming SR&ED ITCs; Section 32 of the Interpretation Act cannot cure the failure to file the prescribed ITC claim schedule.
Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 6
Retroactive consultant summary sheets and failure to record test data

Dismissed SR&ED claims for theatre fire-curtain hydraulic backwind and manual override rigs; held that "Experiment Summary Sheets" created after the fact by an external tax consultant, combined with discarding failed prototypes and failing to measure exact descent times or weights during trials, failed the scientific method and hypothesis tests.
Life Choice Ltd. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 21
Literature reviews without empirical testing do not constitute applied research

Dismissed claims for formulating natural health supplements (laetrile, neuro, and cardio products) where the researcher conducted literature reviews and formulated ingredients "in his mind and on paper" without conducting clinical trials or empirical laboratory experiments.
R. v. Les éléments chauffants Tempora inc., Maged Elhami & Shady Elhami, 2017 QCCQ 2684
Criminal prosecution and sentencing for SR&ED fraud (s. 239(1.1) ITA)

Convicted the corporation and its two principals under paragraphs 239(1.1)(a) and (c) for submitting $4,500,000 in fabricated Pyro Genesis subcontractor invoices to claim $1,324,294 in fraudulent SR&ED ITCs; imposed a fine of $1,324,294 on each of the three co-defendants (totalling $3,972,882) even though the CRA intercepted the fraud before disbursing any refund.
Westsource Group Holdings Inc. v. The Queen, 2018 FCA 57 (aff'g 2017 TCC 9)
Leaving project description boxes blank on Form T661 violates s. 37(11)

Held that filing Form T661 with Lines 240, 242, and 244 left blank failed to provide mandatory "prescribed information" by the 18-month deadline, barring the claim even though a related corporation had already submitted the project narrative to the CRA for the same joint project.
A&D Precision Limited v. The Queen, 2019 TCC 48
System uncertainty in heavy precision machining vs. repairing purchased equipment

Allowed claims for designing an 80-ton CNC horizontal lathe (Project #4) and a double-wheel roll grinding machine (Project #6, even though abandoned due to unresolved vibration), holding that non-trivial combinations of standard technologies at extreme scale created system uncertainty; disallowed costs of attempting to repair defective commercial Tacchi lathes purchased from Italy.
National R&D Inc. v. The Queen, 2020 TCC 47 (aff'd 2022 FCA 72; leave to appeal to SCC dismissed, March 9, 2023, No. 40303)
Self-imposed business constraints vs. technological uncertainty

Dismissed an SR&ED consulting firm's internal software claim ("PTS Project"); held that a business decision to restrict development to outdated software (SQL Server 2000 instead of SQL Server 2005 which already had a native PIVOT command) did not create qualifying technological uncertainty, and retroactively compiled 50-trial summary tables failed the scientific method test.
6398316 Canada Inc. v. The Queen, 2021 TCC 17
Role of economic considerations vs. technological uncertainty

Justice Lafleur affirmed that while business constraints and context are relevant background factors, claimants must frame their hypotheses and uncertainties around technological obstacles rather than purely economic or cost-efficiency objectives.
Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. The Queen, 2021 FCA 88 (aff'g 2019 TCC 246)
Binding authority of Northwest Hydraulic and the "scientific method" criterion

Unanimously rejected the appellant's argument that the absence of the words "scientific method" from the statutory definition of SR&ED eliminated the requirement to follow the scientific method; confirmed that the Northwest Hydraulic criteria remain the appropriate interpretation of the definition under textual, contextual, and purposive statutory interpretation.
CAE Inc. v. His Majesty the King, 2022 FCA 178 (aff'g 2021 TCC 57)
Concessionary repayable government R&D loans constitute government assistance

Unanimously held that non-forgivable loans received under Industry Canada's Strategic Aerospace and Defence Initiative (SADI) for "Project Falcon" at an implicit below-market interest rate constituted government assistance under s. 127(9) and taxable income under s. 12(1)(x), rejecting CAE's attempt to bifurcate the principal loan from the interest rate subsidy.
Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. The King, 2024 TCC / 2025 Amended Reasons (2023-2126(IT)I)
Application of the 5 Northwest Hydraulic criteria to food/beverage formulation

Justice Bodie allowed the taxpayer's 2020 SR&ED appeal for resolving shelf-stability and exploding-can fermentation uncertainties in developing a non-refrigerated beverage ("Chrisoda"), reaffirming Joel Theatrical and Les Abeilles that while contemporaneous documentation is vital to resolve factual disputes, oral and corroborating evidence establishing systematic hypothesis testing satisfies s. 248(1).
Simon Ribbans Photography Inc. v. The King, 2025 TCC 146
Strict 1-year-and-90-day statutory time bar for Notice of Objection extensions

Justice Ouimet denied an extension of time to object where CRA Business Client Communication System (BCCS) and "Print to Mail" affidavits established that the Notices of Assessment were mailed on September 13, 2022 (triggering the irrebuttable presumption of receipt under s. 248(7)), and the taxpayer filed its objection after the 1-year-and-90-day jurisdictional limit in ss. 166.1(7) and 166.2(5) expired.

body.text: 8. Comprehensive Audit Compliance Checklist for Canadian Claimants

To ensure full statutory compliance and audit readiness under the post-Bill C-15 regime, Canadian corporate claimants and tax auditors should verify the following ten operational controls prior to certifying Part 10 of Form T661:

items: Pre-Claim Approval Screening (Before Incurring Costs): For CCPCs, Canadian corporations, and partnerships with annual gross income under $25,000,000, evaluate submitting up to 3 projects through the CRA's Pre-Claim Approval Process in My Business Account to secure a 3-year technical eligibility determination within 8 weeks and qualify for the accelerated 90-day expenditure review standard.

Contemporaneous Technical Evidence Linked to Lines 242, 244, and 246: Maintain dated engineering notebooks, Jira/Git commit histories tagged by SR&ED project code, design of experiments (DOE) matrices, failed prototype logs, and benchmark test data generated as the work progresses to substantiate the "Why" (technological uncertainty relative to the business's knowledge base and attempted advancement) and the "How" (hypothesis formulation, systematic testing, and logical conclusions).

Contemporaneous Project-Level Time Tracking: Require all hands-on technical employees and first-line technical supervisors to maintain contemporaneous weekly or monthly timesheets allocating hours across specific SR&ED project codes versus routine commercial engineering, maintenance, and support.

Specified Employee Cap Verification (2026 YMPE = $74,600): Identify every employee owning ≥10% of any class of shares or dealing at non-arm's length with the corporation; strip 100% of bonuses, profit-based pay, and taxable benefits; cap direct SR&ED wages on Line 305/309 at $373,000 (5 × YMPE under s. 37(9.1)); and cap each specified employee's inclusion in the Part 5 PPA salary base at the lesser of actual SR&ED base salary, 75% of total base salary, and $186,500 (2.5 × YMPE under Reg. 2900(7), filing Form T1174 if shared across associated corporations).

180-Day Accrual Payment Verification (Subsections 78(4) and 127(26)): Audit payroll and accounts payable ledgers prior to the 180th day following fiscal year-end to ensure all accrued SR&ED wages and non-salary SR&ED expenses are paid within 180 days, preventing the permanent loss of the 55% PPA on unpaid wages and the deferral of ITCs on unpaid contractor/material invoices.

Arithmetic Optimization of the Irrevocable Overhead Election (Line 160 vs. Line 162): Before filing Form T661 for the year, model both the 55% Proxy Method (including the Regulation 2900(6) overall cap) and the Traditional Method (Line 360 actual directly related and incremental overhead, including dedicated R&D cloud compute clusters and incremental utilities) to select the method yielding the highest net tax benefit.

Post-December 15, 2024 Capital, SUE, and Lease Substantiation: For depreciable property acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024, maintain contemporaneous equipment usage logs to substantiate whether the asset meets the ≥90% ASA intention test (Lines 380/390, noting that used equipment on Line 390/532 is deductible but earns 0% ITC) or the >50% to <90% SUE actual operating time test (Line 504 at 25% per term for new non-GPOEF, non-PDP equipment), and separate equipment lease costs on Lines 350 and 355 from excluded building rent.

Expenditure Limit Optimization ($6,000,000 Cap & Taxable Capital vs. Gross Revenue Election): For CCPCs whose prior-year associated taxable capital employed in Canada exceeds $15,000,000, calculate the 3-year average consolidated gross revenue across the associated group and elect under subsection 127(10.31) or (10.32) if the gross revenue phase-out yields a higher portion of the $6,000,000 35% enhanced expenditure limit. Ensure Schedule T2SCH49 is filed for all associated CCPCs.

Multi-Provincial Credit Ordering and Strategic Waiver Modelling: Compute provincial R&D credits first (including Quebec's CRIC on Form RD-1029.8.CR-T, Ontario's OITC/ORDTC/OBRITC on Schedules 566/508/568, BC's aligned $6M SR&ED credit on Form T666, Alberta's IEG on AT1 Schedule 29, and Saskatchewan's expanded $2M CCPC credit on Schedule 403), evaluate waiving non-refundable provincial credits (such as the 3.5% Ontario ORDTC under s. 43(1)) if in a tax-loss position, and deduct net provincial assistance from the federal SR&ED base.

Strict 18-Month Statutory Filing Control and Part 9 Disclosure: File the fully completed Form T661 (with all Part 2 boxes 242, 244, and 246 populated and Part 9 claim preparer disclosures completed to avoid the $1,000 s. 162(5.1) penalty) together with Schedule T2SCH31 (or Form T2038(IND)) well in advance of the absolute 18-month corporate reporting deadline (17.5 months for individuals).
